newsitem.title: ITALY: FORECAST - Italy CPI troughs out under 2.0 PCT in Q2.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Italy CPI troughs out under 2.0 PCT in Q2.

text.p: Italian consumer price growth is likely to dip below 2.0 percent in the second quarter of this year but that threshold will signify the trough in the trend of falling inflation, economists said.

A Reuter quarterly poll of 17 analysts showed they expected on average that Italian inflation would touch 1.8-1.9 percent this quarter before inching back over the 2.0 threshold to give an average rate for 1997 of 2.2 percent.
"Domestically the inflation situation will be troughing out in the June figures or if that's not the trough then it will come close to it," said Alex Garrard, European economist at UBS in London.

CPI growth slowed to 2.2 percent year on year in March from 2.4 percent in February and Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said earlier this week it would soon fall to 1.9 percent and could stabilise at 1.5 percent at the end of June.

Lucia Trevisan at Caboto said the 1997 second quarter would compare favourably with the same period in 1996, with gains in food and clothing prices more limited in respect to 1996 as a result of limited demand.

Analysts noted second quarter price growth could end up lower than forecast due to possible changes in electricity prices, currently frozen after the State Council overruled a regional court decision earlier this year to block price rises.

The State Council is due to consider the utility price issue again on May 16 after the expected passage through parliament of a government decree to freeze tariffs in expectation of energy sector reforms. But analysts said if price rises are cancelled this could have an impact of 0.2 percent on the inflation index.

Ken Wattret, economist at Paribas Capital Markets in London, said the broad picture was for inflation to bottom out at the end of the second quarter and then drift up towards 3.0 percent into 1998 which he said should not cause markets concern.

"Inflation now is not a key market mover for Italy. There's a benign outlook for inflation in line with the rest of Europe. As the rate begins to turn back up there may be a few jitters but it won't be going very far," he said.

"It looks like this is one Maastricht criterion that will be met -- in fact it looks likely to be met by southern Europe as a whole. Italy by historical standards is performing exceptionally well but this now is not much of a surprise to markets," he added.

Wattret said as far as producer prices were concerned they would turn up like CPI but would not accelerate rapidly. Paribas saw PPI at 1.2 percent this quarter and inching up gradually over the next two before touching 2.0 percent in early 1998.
The mean of economists' forecasts was for 1.6 percent growth in PPI in the current 1997 quarter, rising to 2.3 by the final three months of the year and creeping up to average 2.6 in 1998.
